description: This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI)–based models for detecting plus disease and treatment-requiring retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) in preterm infants. ROP remains one of the leading causes of preventable childhood blindness, and identification of plus disease is central to treatment decisions. However, assessment based on wide-field digital retinal imaging (WFDRI) is subject to inter-observer variability and depends heavily on the availability of experienced ophthalmic graders. AI-driven image analysis has been proposed as a scalable approach to support screening and improve diagnostic consistency. The review will be conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidance. A comprehensive search will be performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science up to November 2025, with additional screening of reference lists. Eligible studies include original peer-reviewed human investigations evaluating AI algorithms applied to wide-field retinal fundus images, using expert human grading as the reference standard. Outcomes of interest include diagnostic accuracy measures such as sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Study selection, data extraction, and methodological quality assessment will be undertaken independently by multiple reviewers using standardized appraisal tools, including the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for diagnostic test accuracy studies.

title: Deep Learning-Based Analysis of Panoramic and CBCT Images to detect Relations and the Risk of Mandibular third and Inferior Alveolar Nerve: A Scoping Review
description: ABSTRACT Aims: The present scoping review assessed the ability of deep learning (DL) models to determine the relationship between the third mandibular molar (MM3) and the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) using panoramic radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT). The aim was to examine the potential of these models to enhance dental diagnoses of MM3 risk to the nerve. Materials and methods: A systematic literature search encompassed studies published between January 2015 and September 2025 in PubMed, Wiley Online Library, and ScienceDirect. The review included 27 studies which used DL algorithms including the convolutional neural networks, You Only Look Once, ResNet50, AlexNet and RetinaNet to detect and analyze images. Results: The results showed that these models have high accuracy in predicting anatomical relationships with increased diagnostic efficiency compared with manual methods, reducing nerve complication risks from the MM3. The datasets included between 74 and 4,516 X-ray images. The performance metrics included accuracy, F1 score, specificity and sensitivity (Recall). Data heterogeneity including image type, DL architecture and dataset size makes, direct comparison of model performance across studies challenging. Conclusions: DL methods in panoramic radiography and CBCT analysis can improve the accuracy and the efficiency of analyzing the relationship between the MM3 and the IAN, aiding clinical diagnosis and reducing nerve compression risk from wisdom teeth. title: Artificial intelligence in optical coherence tomography and magnetic resonance imaging for optic neuropathies: Scoping Review
description: Introduction: Optic neuropathies are diseases that affect the optic nerve and cause visual loss of varying degrees. Among the most common are glaucoma and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, both major causes of irreversible blindness worldwide. Early diagnosis depends on imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which allow precise evaluation of structural and functional changes in the optic nerve. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool in neuro-ophthalmology, capable of processing large volumes of images with high diagnostic accuracy. However, the rapid expansion of scientific evidence calls for a review that synthesizes current advances, applications, and limitations of this technology. Methodology: A scoping review will be conducted of studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of AI models applied to the analysis of OCT and MRI in optic neuropathies. The search will include databases such as PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, SciELO, and BIREME, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors related to artificial intelligence, deep learning, and optic neuropathies. Grey literature will be included, and the snowball technique will be applied. Expected results: It is expected to generate an updated overview of the evidence on AI in the diagnosis of optic neuropathies, identifying the most used models, their benefits, limitations, and perspectives for clinical integration in neuro-ophthalmology.

title: Public attitudes and acceptance of screening for neurodegenerative disease by AI analysis of retinal OCT images
description: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's are a major and growing cause of disability. As the retina is essentially an outgrowth of the brain, changes in the retina are associated with changes in the brain, which can be viewed via 3D scanning Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), increasingly available in high-street optometrists. Although these changes are often too subtle for the human eye to detect, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning allow for the possibility of screening for neurodegenerative disease as part of a routine eye test, allowing for earlier diagnosis and subsequent treatment. However, this raises the critical question of whether the public would accept such screening. The aim of this study is to determine factors which influence public attitudes to an AI-based screening tool for early signs of neurodegenerative disease, to map a route for improving acceptability and uptake of such a tool based on the results. This study utlises co-creation with a public panel to create an animation role play, simulating a visit to the optometrist. Hypothesised variables to predict uptake include socioeconomic status and uncontrollable mortality risk, whether a human or AI performs the analysis, benefits of screening, proximity to neurodegenerative disease, and demographic factors. Ordinal logistic regression will be applied as the main statistical analysis.

title: The Utility of Central versus Peripheral Visual Field Test Algorithms for Diagnosing Glaucoma: A Scoping Review
description: Glaucoma is a chronic and progressive entity of vision loss that requires detailed monitoring of visual function. In 2013, it was reported that the worldwide prevalence of glaucoma is estimated to be 64.3 million and is expected to increase to 111.8 million in 2040 (Tham YC et al., 2014). In the context of glaucoma diagnosis and management, standard automated perimetry (SAP) is the most utilised investigative technique used by eye health clinicians, with the 24-2 or the 30-2 being the mainstay (Hejil A, et al., 2003). This rationale was adopted under the premise that Glaucoma is a disease affecting the peripheral and mid-peripheral vision in early disease, with changes to central vision only occurring in advanced stages of the disease. Although, with the advent of spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), there is emerging evidence to suggest the macula ganglion cell complex is affected in early disease processes (Hood DC et al., 2011; Hood DC et al., 2013). Hence, there is conjecture as to whether introducing the 10-2 SAP testing algorithm to Glaucoma screening may provide an added benefit in detecting perimetric changes in early Glaucoma (Kim EK et al., 2021). Therefore, in this scoping review our aim is to analyse the literature comparing the 24-2 and 10-2 SAP in the diagnosis of early glaucoma, whilst also assessing the practicability of additional perimetry testing in clinical practice.

title: Vessel Stress Mapping and Preventive Stroke-Risk Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (VSM-ULM)
description: This project builds on recent advances in ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM/sULM) to treat stroke as a mechanical fatigue problem of the microvasculature. Using contrast microbubbles as Lagrangian tracers, we reconstruct the microvascular network and compute vessel-level stress and fragility metrics (Vessel Stress Index, Network Fragility Score) from track-derived features such as velocity, recirculation, normalized distance, and dwell time. To make ULM clinically trustworthy, we propose a Birth-Time Cone Ledger: a physically-constrained, audit-ready multi-object tracker that maintains per-bubble identity with organ-specific speed/acceleration priors and explicit quality flags ("clean / suspicious / broken" trajectories). On the sensing side, we outline a stress-reporting tracer concept: a second-layer contrast agent (shear- or inflammation-responsive) that irreversibly changes its US/PA signal in mechanically or biochemically stressed segments. Its per-segment signal (SRI) is fused with the ULM-derived stress metrics into a Composite Risk Index for each vessel. Finally, we specify a cheap, CEUS-based clinical workflow that runs on existing high-end ultrasound systems, with realistic scan times, GPU-accelerated processing, coverage/QC reporting, and simple outputs (heatmaps + scores) suitable for preventive screening and follow-up in high-risk patients. What is new compared to current research – We turn ULM track data into an explicit microvascular fatigue geometry (VSI + NFS), rather than only mapping perfusion or velocity. – We introduce a physically-gated tracking ledger tailored for clinical auditability, complementary to existing Kalman/GLMB/LSTM tracking schemes. – We frame stress-responsive contrast as a diagnostic, repeatable "risk paint" layer on top of CEUS, instead of purely theranostic nanoparticles. – We design a full, low-cost stroke-risk exam that could realistically be implemented on current CEUS equipment, rather than a single algorithm or phantom study.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Surrogate for Electroretinography in Cone Dystrophy: A Feasibility Framework
description: This project registers a feasibility framework exploring whether artificial intelligence (AI) models applied to multimodal retinal imaging can predict electroretinography (ERG)–defined cone dysfunction in cone dystrophy. Full-field ERG remains the gold standard for assessing cone photoreceptor function; however, access to ERG is limited in many clinical and low-resource settings. This framework proposes the use of widely available imaging modalities—optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence (FAF)—combined with convolutional neural network–based models to infer whether cone-specific ERG parameters (photopic single-flash and 30 Hz flicker responses) fall within or outside normal limits. The project is designed as a methodological and conceptual feasibility exercise rather than a confirmatory study. It does not aim to replace ERG, predict raw ERG waveforms, or commit to a predefined dataset or sample size. Instead, it documents a structured approach for investigating structure–function relationships in inherited retinal diseases using AI, particularly in ERG-limited environments. An abstract based on this framework has been accepted into the scientific program of the 40th World Ophthalmology Congress (WOC 2026), to be held in Prague, Czech Republic, under the topic Artificial Intelligence and Telemedicine, as an E-Poster Viewing presentation (poster identifier PV-AI-033), titled "Artificial Intelligence as a Surrogate for Electroretinography in Cone Dystrophy Diagnosis: A Feasibility Framework." description: Background: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique capable of measuring epidermal thickness (ET) in vivo by detecting the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ). Objective: This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature to identify demographic (e.g., age, sex, skin type), anatomical (e.g., body site, skin features), pathological (e.g., skin disease), and technical/operator-related factors that influence the ability of OCT to visualize the DEJ and obtain a reliable ET measurement. Rationale: Understanding which factors impair or preserve OCT-based ET measurement is essential for guiding clinical deployment, informing study design, and identifying populations or anatomical sites where alternative imaging approaches may be necessary. No existing review has comprehensively synthesized these factors across both healthy and diseased skin. Methods: A scoping review will be conducted and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search of relevant databases will identify studies examining OCT-based ET measurement or DEJ visualization across varying patient demographics, anatomical sites, skin conditions, and imaging protocols.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.

title: Predicting Stroke Risk Using Retinal Imaging with Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence
description: Stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, with a substantial proportion of cases considered preventable through early risk identification and targeted interventions. Traditional stroke risk prediction models rely primarily on clinical and demographic variables and demonstrate only moderate predictive performance, often failing to capture subclinical vascular changes. In recent years, advances in retinal imaging and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the non-invasive assessment of microvascular and neurovascular alterations that may reflect underlying cerebrovascular risk. The retina shares anatomical and physiological characteristics with cerebral vasculature, making it a promising window for stroke risk assessment. As a growing body of literature explores AI-based analysis of retinal images for predicting stroke and related cerebrovascular outcomes, a comprehensive mapping of the existing evidence is needed. This scoping review protocol outlines the planned methods to systematically identify, characterize, and synthesize current research on the use of retinal imaging combined with artificial intelligence for stroke risk prediction.

title: The Current Status of OCT and OCTA Imaging for the Diagnosis of Long COVID
description: This systematic review explores the potential of optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in diagnosing long COVID. Long term effects of the COVID-19 disease could impact the microvascular system, which can be visualized directly through changes in vessel density and foveal avascular zone in OCTA and indirectly in the form of retinal layer thicknesses in OCT. This review shows a summarized comparison of all 24 topic-related clinical studies of adult participants, collected in the database PubMed and, with the AI research assistant Elicit published in the period between February 2021 and March 2024. Studies with participant groups of patients with active COVID-19, recovered participants and participants with ongoing symptoms were included. During the various stages of COVID-19, retinal changes could be observed, but a comparison between long COVID and recovered cohorts was aggravated by diverse inclusion and exclusion criteria as well as small sample sizes. Changes in long COVID were seen in most OCT examinations as thinning or partial thinning of certain retinal layers, while in OCTA a consistently reduced vessel density was revealed.

title: In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy in the Diagnosis and Management of Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia: A Scoping Review
description: Purpose: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) encompasses a spectrum of premalignant and malignant epithelial lesions of the conjunctiva and cornea. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective management and prevention of recurrence. In-vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) has emerged as a promising, noninvasive imaging tool that provides real-time, high-resolution visualization of the ocular surface at the cellular level. Despite growing interest, the literature on IVCM's diagnostic accuracy, characteristic imaging features, and clinical utility in OSSN remains fragmented. This scoping review aims to systematically identify, chart, and synthesize the existing evidence on the application of IVCM in OSSN. It will examine how IVCM has been used to detect, characterize, and monitor OSSN lesions; assess correlations between IVCM and histopathology; and explore its integration with complementary imaging modalities such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM). The review will also map methodological limitations and research gaps to inform future clinical and technological advancements in ocular oncology imaging. Expected Outcomes: The review will produce a comprehensive summary of current knowledge on the diagnostic and monitoring role of IVCM in OSSN. It will: Identify characteristic IVCM features associated with various OSSN grades. Evaluate the strengths, limitations, and diagnostic accuracy of IVCM compared to standard histopathology. Highlight how IVCM has been applied in monitoring treatment response and disease recurrence. Identify knowledge gaps and propose directions for future studies, including the potential role of artificial intelligence in automating IVCM image analysis. Overall, this review will serve as a foundational reference for clinicians and researchers, clarifying the present and potential roles of IVCM in OSSN diagnosis and management, and guiding the development of noninvasive, multimodal imaging approaches in ocular surface oncology.

title: Systematic Audit of Public Ophthalmic Imaging Datasets: Assessment of Transparency, Fairness, Usability, and Reproducibility for Machine-Learning Research
description: This project is a systematic audit of publicly available ophthalmic imaging datasets used in machine-learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) research. Its purpose is to evaluate the extent to which existing datasets support transparent, fair, reproducible, and clinically meaningful AI development. Although ophthalmology is a leading domain for clinical AI, many studies rely on datasets with inconsistent documentation, unclear licensing, limited demographic reporting, variable label quality, and data-splitting practices that may compromise reproducibility and validity. This project aims to systematically characterize these datasets and assess their readiness for clinical ML applications. Using a pre-registered protocol, the study will identify eligible datasets through bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and dataset and code repositories. The dataset will be the unit of analysis, with multiple publications or repository pages describing the same dataset consolidated into a single record. Standardized data extraction will capture information on accessibility and licensing, imaging modalities and technical specifications, annotation and labeling practices, demographic transparency, dataset structure, reproducibility features, and evidence of maintenance or versioning. Each dataset will be evaluated using a structured, multi-domain readiness scorecard designed to assess usability, transparency, fairness, and reproducibility. Scoring domains include accessibility and licensing clarity, documentation quality, label quality and inter-rater reliability, demographic reporting, technical completeness, fairness indicators, split hygiene, maintenance and versioning, and clinical and modality diversity. Domain scores will be aggregated to generate an interpretable readiness score that enables comparison across datasets and clinical tasks. Expected outcomes include a curated inventory of public ophthalmic imaging datasets, a transparent framework for evaluating dataset readiness, and descriptive analyses highlighting strengths, limitations, and gaps in the current ophthalmic AI data landscape. Findings will inform best-practice recommendations for dataset development and reporting and support more robust and equitable clinical AI research.

title: Leading Towards a Translation Readiness Framework: A Systematic Review of Deep Learning Approaches for Eye Diseases Diagnosis
description: Background: Artificial intelligence has significantly improved the diagnosis of retinal diseases using fundus and optical coherence tomography. However, the pathway between the accuracy of the models and their clinical application is still unclear. Objectives: The main objective of this systematic review is to overcome this gap by correlating the quality of methodology with clinical preparation in the current studies and to critically examine the translation readiness possibility. Methods: The PRISMA-based review clearly addresses the six research questions in an organized manner. A comprehensive search is conducted across six electronic databases, resulting in a total of 883 records. After rigorous screening, a final set of 43 fundus- and OCT-based articles published between 2020 and August 2025 and passing a comprehensive eligibility criterion are selected. The selected studies are assessed using the custom AI-specific risk-of-bias assessment tool and the CLAIM checklist to measure the quality of technical reporting. The reviewer's agreement is calculated using Cohen's kappa, interrater reliability, and the intraclass correlation coefficient. Results: Although convolutional and hybrid deep-learning-based studies are often reported to have an accuracy of more than 95.0%, only 14.3% are truly clinically validated, and 23.1% do not include code or implementation data details. Reviewers' agreement scores are from moderate to high (fundus-based ICC(2,1)=0.911, ICC(2,1)=0.911,CI=[0.896,0.923]) and (OCT based ICC(2,1)=0.643, CI=[0.422,0.792]), supporting the reliability of the quality assessments. In order to combine these dimensions, we come up with a composite Technical-Clinical Integrity Index, which measures data transparency, rigor of validation, and reporting of performance. Conclusion: Retinal disease diagnosis has achieved high performance with low clinical transfer. This review provides the guidelines of a Translational Readiness Framework that can be used by researchers, clinicians, and health-analytics teams to assess and implement credible artificial intelligence systems in ophthalmology.

title: Use of the Keratograph® 5M for the Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease: A Scoping Review
description: Dry Eye Disease (DED) is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterized by tear film instability and associated ocular symptoms. Objective assessment of tear film parameters and meibomian gland function is essential for accurate diagnosis and subtype classification. In recent years, non-invasive imaging technologies have been increasingly incorporated into clinical practice to enhance diagnostic precision and reduce variability associated with traditional tests. The Keratograph® 5M (Oculus Optikgeräte GmbH, Germany) is a Placido-disc–based corneal topographer that integrates automated, non-contact measurements of tear film stability and ocular surface parameters. The device provides non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT), tear meniscus height (TMH), meibography, ocular redness quantification, and additional surface analyses. Although widely used in ophthalmology and optometry settings, the scope, consistency, and characteristics of the published evidence regarding its diagnostic application in DED have not been comprehensively mapped. The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and synthesize the available scientific literature evaluating the use of the Keratograph® 5M in the diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease. Specifically, this review aims to: (1) map the clinical contexts in which the device has been studied; (2) describe the tear film and glandular parameters assessed; (3) summarize reported measurement properties (e.g., repeatability, reproducibility); and (4) identify research gaps related to diagnostic performance and clinical implementation. This review will follow established methodological guidance for scoping reviews and will include peer-reviewed primary studies evaluating the Keratograph® 5M in adult or mixed populations undergoing assessment for DED or related ocular surface conditions. Data extraction will focus on study design, population characteristics, diagnostic parameters evaluated, reference standards (when applicable), and key findings. No formal meta-analysis is planned, as the objective is evidence mapping rather than quantitative synthesis. Expected outcomes include a structured overview of the current evidence landscape, identification of methodological heterogeneity in diagnostic assessment, and clarification of how the Keratograph® 5M is positioned within the diagnostic pathway of DED. The findings may inform future diagnostic accuracy studies, health technology assessments, and clinical guideline development.

title: Performance and limitation of machine learning algorithms for diabetic retinopathy screening and its application in health management: a meta-analysis
description: Diabetes mellitus affects 463 million adults and consumes 1.8% of gross domestic product globally, posing a huge burden on healthcare systems, especially in remote, underserved areas. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a vision-threatening condition that affects 22.27% of adults with diabetes. With the diabetes pandemic spreading from wealthy industrialized countries to developing regions, the number of people with DR will increase from 103.12 million in 2020 to 160.50 million in 2045. Visual impairment and blindness due to DR can be significantly reduced if diagnosed at an early stage and treated appropriately. However, due to the high cost and low accessibility of eye services, <70% of people with diabetes receive eye examinations at regular intervals. The current strategy for detecting DR is based on clinical examination by an ophthalmologist or grading of retinal photographs via telemedicine, which relies on highly trained staff or requires expensive equipment. In addition, whether the recommended screening interval can be extended has attracted extensive debate because a large number of DR-negative patients receive repeated annual fundus screenings. It was estimated that the DR service would be reduced by 40% if people with no visible retinopathy at two consecutive screens received 2-year rather than annual screening in the Scottish Diabetic Retinopathy Screening programme. The National Health Service Foundation Trust claimed that screening people with type 2 diabetes every 2 years, rather than annually, would reduce screening costs by 25%. Therefore, establishing simple, practical methods for identifying people at high risk of referable DR (RDR) based on easily accessible indicators has become an important goal, which will help to target screening and prevention. Modeling for RDR is challenging because most medical data has a non-linear, non-normal, and non-independent distribution, and traditional regression analysis techniques would lose information. The use of machine learning (ML) techniques offers an alternative solution, which captures the non-linear relationship in data without prior assumption. Furthermore, ML is able to rank variables by importance. Previous studies have demonstrated that ML-based methods can accurately identify diabetes in the general population. However, limited studies based on ML for DR classification are available to date.

title: Diabetic retinopathy in primary health care: a narrative review
description: ABSTRACT Objective: This review aims to summarize the most relevant information on diabetic retinopathy (DR), a common preventable complication of diabetes, highlighting the key role of the primary care physician in its timely detection and management. Design and Methodology: A narrative review of the scientific literature published in the last decade was conducted. Study selection: original articles, reviews, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and grey literature providing current and relevant data were included; ultimately, 43 references were selected after critical analysis, compiling information on prevalence, risk factors, pathophysiological mechanisms, prevention strategies, diagnosis, and treatment. Results: DR affects more than one in five adults with diabetes, and its prevalence continues to rise. Careful control of blood glucose, blood pressure, and lipid levels, along with regular screening and patient education, are the most effective tools to prevent visual loss. Additionally, objective assessment of visual acuity (VA) and systematic fundus examination are essential for early detection and appropriate monitoring of the disease. Current therapies, such as anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) agents and laser photocoagulation, have improved the prognosis of advanced cases. Conclusions: DR can be effectively prevented and treated if detected early. The general practitioner, with a comprehensive and interdisciplinary approach, plays a fundamental role in reducing the impact of this disease and improving the quality of life of people with diabetes. description: Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most prevalent complications of diabetes mellitus (DM) and one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. title: Artificial intelligence applications in fundus photograph image analysis for diagnosis and screening of brain tumours: A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review aims to evaluate the utility and diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning algorithms applied to fundus and retinal imaging for the detection, diagnosis, and screening of brain tumours and related intracranial pathologies. Brain tumours, including gliomas, pituitary neoplasms, and other intracranial neoplasms, often present with ocular signs such as papilloedema and other optic nerve head abnormalities that can be detected through fundus photography. Early identification of these signs via non-invasive retinal imaging has the potential to facilitate timely diagnosis and improve patient outcomes. The primary purpose of this review is to synthesise current evidence on the performance of AI-based diagnostic tools in analysing retinal images to identify brain tumours and their associated ocular manifestations. Specifically, the review will assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI algorithms - measured by sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - in diverse clinical and screening settings. It will also examine the potential of these technologies to improve early detection, screening processes, and clinical decision-making compared to conventional methods, such as clinical examination and neuroimaging. The review will include original research studies, including diagnostic accuracy studies, cohort studies, case-control studies, and observational reports, that have evaluated AI/ML models applied to fundus or retinal photographs. The studies will be scrutinised for quality and bias using the QUADAS-2 tool to ensure robustness of findings. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI in this context, identification of knowledge gaps, and recommendations for future research and clinical practice. Ultimately, this review aims to inform stakeholders - including clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers - about the feasibility and accuracy of integrating AI-based retinal image analysis into routine screening and diagnostic pathways for brain tumours.

description: Epiretinal membrane is a common retinal condition, particularly in the elderly, than can lead to reduced visual acuity and visual distortion. title: Ultrasonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Measurement Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC) : Scoping Literature Review
description: The optic nerve is surrounded by the same meningeal coverings that surround the brain. This anatomic relationship allows the use of Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) as a non-invasive, bedside estimate of elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP). Despite the increasing research interest in ultrasonographic ONSD, it is not widely used clinically. This can be due to variability in ONSD measurements as identified by several meta-analyses that showed significant heterogeneity in ONSD measurement techniques. We propose that this heterogeneity is due to lack of consensus on ONSD measurement technique, which can cause variations in image acquisition and measurement. In this review, We will identify published ONSD imaging and measurement criteria through a scoping systematic review of ultrasound ONSD studies. We will use a piloted data sheet to extract ONSD imaging and measurement criteria. We will then use the output of the review to develop a checklist for ONSD Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC). This checklist will undergo further refinement in the future by using the modified Delphi method to reach expert consensus on ONSD quality criteria.

title: DEEP LEARNING FOR AUTOMATED DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION OF TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description: Title: Deep Learning for Automated Detection and Classification of Temporomandibular Joint Disorders: A Scoping Review Temporomandibular Joint Disorders (TMDs) are a significant clinical challenge associated with pain, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life. Traditional diagnostic approaches—such as manual interpretation of MRI, CBCT, CT, or panoramic images—can be time-consuming, subjective, and affected by inter-observer variability. With recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) techniques, automated detection and classification of TMDs has emerged as a promising solution to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. This scoping review systematically maps current evidence on deep learning applications for diagnosing TMDs, including anterior disc displacement (ADD), osteoarthritis, condylar degeneration, and degenerative joint disease. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search across PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and Wiley identified 15 eligible studies published between 2015 and 2025. Across these studies, models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), U-Net, ResNet, VGG16, MobileNetV2, YOLO, and ensemble architectures demonstrated high diagnostic performance—achieving accuracy levels up to 99%, sensitivity up to 98%, and significant improvements in segmentation precision. Findings indicate that deep learning can reduce diagnostic time by up to 50%, standardize interpretation, and serve as an effective decision-support tool for clinicians. Despite promising results, challenges remain related to dataset diversity, external validation, reproducibility, and clinical integration. Future research should focus on multi-center datasets, multimodal learning, standardized benchmarking, explainability methods such as Grad-CAM, and ethical frameworks for AI deployment in healthcare. This review highlights the potential of deep learning to transform TMD diagnostics, contributing to faster, more accurate, and more consistent radiologic evaluation, ultimately improving clinical outcomes for patients.

title: Age-Specific Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Cut-Off Values for Detecting Raised Intracranial Pressure in Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This study aims to systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and age-specific cut-off values of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured using ultrasonography for detecting raised intracranial pressure (ICP) in pediatric populations. Raised ICP is a critical condition in children with neurological disorders, including traumatic brain injury, hydrocephalus, infections, and intracranial tumors. Non-invasive bedside techniques such as ONSD ultrasonography have gained increasing attention as potential screening tools for early ICP detection. A systematic review and diagnostic meta-analysis were conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Multiple electronic databases were searched to identify relevant studies evaluating ONSD as a diagnostic marker for raised ICP in children. Eligible studies included pediatric participants aged 0–18 years and reported diagnostic accuracy data comparing ONSD measurements with reference standards such as invasive intracranial pressure monitoring, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or lumbar puncture. Data extracted from included studies comprised study characteristics, participant demographics, diagnostic thresholds, and diagnostic accuracy parameters including sensitivity, specificity, true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. A hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model and random-effects meta-analysis were used to estimate pooled diagnostic accuracy. The study also explores age-specific variations in ONSD cut-off values across pediatric age groups. The findings aim to support clinical decision-making and provide evidence for the use of ONSD ultrasonography as a non-invasive screening tool for raised intracranial pressure in children.

title: Desempeño diagnóstico de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto: una revisión sistemática exploratoria
description: El glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto (GPAA) es una neuropatía óptica crónica y progresiva caracterizada por daño del nervio óptico y pérdida de la capa de fibras nerviosas retinianas, lo que conduce a defectos irreversibles del campo visual y constituye una de las principales causas de ceguera irreversible a nivel mundial (1,2). Se estima que su prevalencia global en adultos oscila entre 2.4% y 3.0%, con variaciones importantes según edad, origen étnico y factores genéticos (3,4). El diagnóstico temprano del GPAA representa un desafío clínico importante debido a la variabilidad interobservador en la evaluación del nervio óptico y la interpretación de pruebas diagnósticas como la fotografía de fondo de ojo, la tomografía de coherencia óptica (OCT) y los campos visuales computarizados (5,6). Además, el acceso limitado a especialistas en oftalmología en muchos sistemas de salud, particularmente en regiones de ingresos medios y bajos, contribuye al subdiagnóstico de la enfermedad (7,8). En este contexto, los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA), particularmente aquellos basados en aprendizaje automático (machine learning) y aprendizaje profundo (deep learning), han emergido como herramientas prometedoras para mejorar la precisión y eficiencia del diagnóstico del glaucoma. Diversos estudios han demostrado que algoritmos basados en redes neuronales convolucionales pueden alcanzar sensibilidades y especificidades superiores al 90% en la detección de neuropatía óptica glaucomatosa utilizando imágenes de fondo de ojo y OCT (9–12). Sin embargo, la literatura disponible presenta heterogeneidad metodológica en términos de diseños de estudio, poblaciones evaluadas, estándares de referencia y modalidades diagnósticas utilizadas, lo que dificulta la síntesis estructurada de la evidencia sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de estos sistemas (13,14). El objetivo de esta revisión sistemática exploratoria es mapear y sintetizar la evidencia disponible sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de sistemas de inteligencia artificial comparados con métodos diagnósticos convencionales en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto. La revisión seguirá la metodología del Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) para revisiones de alcance y las directrices PRISMA-ScR, incluyendo estudios publicados entre enero de 2020 y marzo de 2026 (15,16). Se realizará una búsqueda sistemática en las bases de datos PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science y BIREME/BVS. Dos revisores independientes realizarán la selección de estudios y la extracción de datos, y el riesgo de sesgo será evaluado mediante la herramienta QUADAS-AI (17,18). Los resultados se sintetizarán mediante análisis descriptivo y narrativo de las métricas de precisión diagnóstica reportadas, incluyendo sensibilidad, especificidad, valores predictivos, exactitud diagnóstica y área bajo la curva ROC. Esta revisión permitirá caracterizar el estado actual de la evidencia sobre la aplicación clínica de la inteligencia artificial en el diagnóstico del GPAA, así como identificar brechas de conocimiento relevantes para futuras investigaciones y estrategias de implementación clínica. title: Minimum Semantic Content (MSC) image dataset, a balanced dataset containing "ugly" images (alongside more traditionally appealing ones) of objects with little semantic content
description: The Minimum Semantic Content (MSC) dataset provides a structured resource aimed at isolating aesthetic judgments from cognitive (semantic) influences, making it particularly useful for advancing empirical studies on aesthetics. Unlike existing image datasets that predominantly feature beautiful images, the MSC dataset offers a balanced selection of 10,426 images, carefully curated span the whole range from "ugly" to "beautiful". The images were also selected to minimize semantic content. This reduction allows researchers to focus on perceptual factors underlying aesthetic judgments, avoiding the confounding influence of complex cognitive associations. Each image in the MSC dataset has been evaluated by 100 observers, ensuring robust data on aesthetic ratings. By including comparable amounts of "beautiful" and "ugly" images, the MSC dataset enables a re-examination of relationships between low-level image features and aesthetic valuations. This expanded aesthetic range offers insights that challenge or refine current models, demonstrating that limiting datasets to predominantly beautiful images can skew, exaggerate, or miss significant findings on the aesthetic response to image content. Each of the 10,426 images in the MSC dataset has been evaluated by 100 observers, ensuring robust data on aesthetic ratings. By including a method for generating "ugly" images alongside more traditionally appealing ones, the MSC dataset enables a re-examination of relationships between low-level image features and aesthetic valuations. We provide a .csv file with raw crowdsourcing results, with each column representing the number of votes received for each of the five aesthetic valuation categories (1 = very ugly, 5 = very beautiful). we also provide results from truncated histogram fittings to the crowdsourcing data. These columns include the final value of mu (mean), the final value of sigma (standard deviation), the final FVAL and ExitFlag values from Matlab's fminsearch function, and the number of iterations required. Images were modified by observers. We provide categorization columns, specifying whether an image is "uglified," "beautified," "auto_uglified," or "unmodified." This section also indicates if an image served as the starting point for a modification (e.g., "uglified_original" denotes an image used as the basis for an uglification process). This structure ensures that users can easily identify the type and provenance of each image, as well as access comprehensive metadata and aesthetic ratings for further analysis.

title: Quality evaluation indicators for Ophthalmic nursing: a scoping review
description: OBJECTIVE: To conduct a scoping review of the literature related to ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation indexes, systematically sort out the current situation of the construction of ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation indexes at home and abroad, and aim to provide theoretical basis for the establishment of a scientific, standardised ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation system with specialised characteristics. METHODS: Eleven domestic and international databases were systematically searched according to the scope review framework proposed by JBI. The search time frame was established until May 2025, and two researchers independently screened the literature and classified and analysed the content of the indicators based on the three-dimensional quality structure model. RESULTS: A total of 28 papers were included in this study. The highest frequency of ophthalmic care quality indicator application scenarios was in ophthalmic wards, the most common ophthalmic speciality care quality indicator was glaucoma, and ophthalmic speciality care quality indicators were mainly centred around forced body position. The evaluation indicators were categorised according to the three-dimensional quality structure model, and the evaluation indicators appeared 491 times cumulatively, of which 134 times (27.29%) were structural quality-related indicators, 235 times (47.86%) were process-quality-related indicators, and 122 times (24.85%) were outcome-quality-related indicators.42.2% of the tertiary-level indicators had problems such as unclear definitions. In terms of indicator content, foreign studies placed more emphasis on disease management and patient-reported outcomes. CONCLUSION: The existing ophthalmic care quality indicator system is still insufficient in terms of specialty specificity and operability. In the future, we should strengthen the clarity of the definition of the indicators and the consistency of the measurement standards, highlight the professional characteristics of ophthalmic care, and promote the establishment of a logical, scientifically rigorous, and practically valuable ophthalmic care quality evaluation system.

title: Central Contrast sensitivity as an outcome measure in randomised controlled trials in glaucoma – a systematic review
description: Contrast sensitivity is an important aspect of visual function. It has previously been shown to decline in the early stages of glaucoma. To our knowledge, no systematic review has yet to be written on the topic of glaucoma and contrast sensitivity. It is important to synthesise the existing evidence in order to inform the use of these tests in future research and clinical practice. As a start, we want to investigate the use of central contrast sensitivity tests in RCTs on glaucoma. Whether they are used as primary or secondary outcomes, what types of tests are used, the format of data outcome, method of aggregation, time points used, baseline and endpoint contrast sensitivity values. We plan a descriptive synthesis of the results.

description: ReVis-MD is an interdisciplinary project aimed at better understanding functional adaptation following the onset of scotoma in patients with macular degeneration (MD). By combining ophthalmological, psychophysical, neural (fMRI), and neuro-computational (artificial neural networks) approaches, the project pursues two main objectives. The first is to characterize the cortical reorganizations occurring in patients and how these changes impact their visuo-cognitive abilities, such as scene processing, compared to an age-matched control group with an artificial central scotoma. The second objective is to assess whether these adaptations can be enhanced through perceptual learning and cognitive retraining strategies, potentially paving the way for future rehabilitation programs. description: Inherited retinal dystrophies (IRDs) are a large family of rare eye diseases that lead to gradual impairment of color perception and night vision, to peripheral or central visual field deficits and ultimately to blindness even from a young age. Patient Reported Outcome Measures (PROMs) are tools in the form of questionnaires, designed to reflect how a patient feels or performs. Ideally, they should undergo psychometric validation to ensure that they accurately capture what they intend to measure and can reliably assess change over time. This scoping review aims to present what PROM tools are being used in clinical trials and observational studies regarding IRDs in the last decade.

title: Diagnostic Selective Nerve Root Block (SNRB) in Lumbar Nerve Root Compression
description: Background and Aim Selective nerve root blocks (SNRBs) are widely used in spine surgery for diagnostic clarification in patients with radicular pain, particularly when imaging (MRI) and clinical findings are inconclusive regarding the symptomatic nerve root or the expected benefit of surgical decompression. The purpose of the block is to clarify the diagnosis and prognosis of radiating lower limb pain, thereby supporting decision-making regarding surgical versus non-surgical treatment. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the prognostic value of selective nerve root blocks in lumbar nerve root compression. Objectives and Hypotheses Primary objective: To assess whether patients undergoing surgery after a diagnostic block with good effect demonstrate different postoperative outcomes, measured by the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at 12 months, compared with patients undergoing surgery without a prior block, adjusted for relevant confounders. Hypothesis: Patients with a positive diagnostic block who subsequently undergo surgery experience less postoperative improvement, measured by ODI, compared with patients undergoing surgery without prior diagnostic uncertainty. Study Design Retrospective cohort study based on registry data and medical records. Population and Eligibility Criteria Inclusion criteria: - Patients aged >18 years - Underwent diagnostic selective lumbar nerve root block (BAFA7) between January 1, 2018 and May 31, 2024 at Zealand University Hospital, Køge Exclusion criteria: - Therapeutic (non-diagnostic) blocks - Missing data regarding block level, side, effect, or subsequent surgery - Missing 12‐month follow-up in DaneSpine - Surgery performed at a different spinal level than the block Data Sources and Variables Primary data sources include the Health Platform, private hospital records, and DaneSpine. Collected variables include demographics, block characteristics, surgical details, and PROM data (ODI, VAS, EQ‐5D). Outcome Measures Primary outcome: - ODI at 12 months postoperatively Secondary outcomes: - Patient satisfaction - Likelihood ratios and predictive values - Avoided surgery following negative block - Re-referral to the spine clinic at any time during follow-up Statistical Analysis Mixed-effects linear regression models will be applied. Fixed effects include block status and relevant covariates, while patient ID is included as a random effect. Ethical Considerations This retrospective registry study involves no patient contact and has been approved in accordance with the Danish Health Act §46.2 and 5, EMN-2025-04765. Data handling complies with GDPR regulations and the project is registered at the institutional registry for research projects, p-2025-19418 Timeline Protocol and approvals: March–August 2025 Data extraction: September–January 2026 Analysis: February 2026 Manuscript preparation: February - June 2026 Publication Plan Results will be published open access. Authorship follows ICMJE guidelines.

title: The Kvasir-Capsule Dataset
description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is predicted to have profound effects on the future of video capsule endoscopy (VCE) technology. The potential lies in improving anomaly detection while reducing manual labour. However, medical data is often sparse and unavailable to the research community, and qualified medical personnel rarely have time for the tedious labelling work. In this respect, we present Kvasir-Capsule, a large VCE dataset collected from examinations at Hospitals in Norway. Kvasir-Capsule consists of 117 videos which can be used to extract a total of 4,741,504 image frames. We have labelled and medically verified 47,238 frames with a bounding box around detected anomalies from 14 different classes of findings. In addition to these labelled images, there are 4,694,266 unlabelled frames included in the dataset. Initial work demonstrates the potential benefits ofAI-based computer-assisted diagnosis systems for VCE. However, they also show that there is great potential for improvements, and the Kvasir-Capsule dataset can play a valuable role in developing better algorithms in order for VCE technology to reach its true potential.

description: Artificial intelligence is currently a hot topic in medicine. The fact that medical data is often sparse for various reasons leads to technical limitations. In this respect, we share the HyperKvasir dataset, which is the largest multi-class image and video dataset from the gastrointestinal tract available today. The data is collected during real gastro- and colonoscopy examinations at a Hospital in Norway and partly labeled by experienced gastrointestinal endoscopists. The dataset contains 110,079 images and 374 videos where it captures anatomical landmarks and pathological and normal findings giving in total around 1 million images and video frames. A zip of the complete dataset can be downloaded at https://datasets.simula.no/hyper-kvasir The paper describing the dataset (which should be cited when the dataset is used), is found here: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-020-00622-y Additional data created by the experiments and source code can be found in this Github repository: https://github.com/simula/hyper-kvasir

title: Use of deep learning-based optic chiasm segmentation for the investigation of visual system pathophysiology and neuroplasticity
description: Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models are of great promise to aid segmentation and analysis of brain structures. Here, we tested, whether CNN trained to segment normal optic chiasms from T1w MRI image can be also applied to abnormal chiasms, specifically with optic nerve misrouting as typical for human albinism. We performed supervised training of the CNN on the T1w images of control participants (n=1049) from Human Connectome Project repository and automatically generated algorithm-based optic chiasm masks. The trained CNN was subsequently tested on data of persons with albinism (PWA; n=9) and controls (n=8) from the CHIASM repository. The quality of outcome segmentation was assessed via the comparison to manually defined optic chiasm masks using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The results revealed contrasting quality of masks obtained for control (mean DSC ± SEM = 0.75 ± 0.03) and PWA data (0.43 ± 0.8, FWE corrected p=0.04). The fact that the CNN recognition of the optic chiasm fails for chiasm abnormalities in PWA underlines the fundamental differences in their spatial features. This finding thus provides proof-of-concept for a novel deep-learning based diagnostics-approach of chiasmal misrouting from T1w images, as well as further analyses on chiasmal misrouting and their impact on structure and function of visual system.

description: Arterial stiffness (AS) is a well-established index of macrovascular damage and predicts cardiovascular complications in many diseases including diabetes mellitus (DM). We included studies with adult patients diagnosed with type 1 or 2 DM, which evaluated the correlation of AS and impaired microcirculation. AS could be evaluated with pulse wave velocity (PWV), carotid-ankle vascular index (CAVI), ambulatory arterial stiffness index (AASI) and augmentation index (Aix). Impaired microcirculation was defined by the presence of one or more of the following: retinopathy, albuminuria, neuropathy, dermal capillary alterations.

title: Noninvasive Measurement of Retinal Dopamine Levels Using Electroretinography: A Novel Approach
description: Dopamine is a crucial neuromodulator in the retina, involved in various visual functions, including adaptation to light, color perception, and circadian rhythms. It is also one of the basic neuromodulators that influences the sensitivity to spatial frequencies of the visual field. Traditional methods of studying retinal dopamine levels, such as post-mortem analysis and animal models, limit the understanding of its real-time role and dynamics in vivo. Electroretinograms (ERG) provide a non-invasive means to study retinal function, but their capability to reflect dopamine levels indirectly through specific wave components is underexplored. Recent advances in vitreous analysis techniques offer a new avenue to quantify dopamine metabolites, like DOPAC and homovanillic acid, which could correlate with ERG findings. This study aims to bridge the gap in methodology by combining ERG with biochemical analysis of the vitreous humor from patients undergoing vitrectomy, potentially unveiling a novel, non-invasive biomarker for retinal dopamine activity.

description: According to the World Health Organization, some of the leading causes of vision impairment and blindness are; Refractive errors Cataract Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Age-related macular degeneration A majority of these conditions requires referrals to ophthalmologists resulting in extended waiting times, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. This systematic review showcases a variety of automated pupilometers that can be used for such diagnosis. With the great advancement in technology, currently, also smartphones can be a possible accessible, affordable and easy-to-use solution to screen for such conditions. Overall, this review aims to investigate the pupillometry variables that are significantly affected by the aforementioned conditions. This can the inform the design of novel dedicated software and hardware. In summary, a systematic literature review was carried out, yielding 51 relevant studies. Among the significant variables there were constriction amplitude, velocity, duration and latency.

title: 2COD: Ocular Dominance Measure
description: It is simple to determine which is a person's more dominant eye. However, outside clinical settings it is currently difficult to assign a reliable objective magnitude to the degree of dominance. For this reason, it is difficult to determine the relation between ocular dominance (O.D.) and cognitive functions that may share a common basis. Here we evaluate a mathematical model of O.D from which we derive a quantitative Index of O.D. The Index is produced by having participants reproduce, on a computer monitor, the outline of a solid disk positioned between themselves and said monitor under three conditions: with both eyes open and with only one of the eyes open. From these drawings we derive a new ocular dominance measure which we call two-camera-ocular-dominance (2COD). We quantify the test-retest reliability of 2COD, and also evaluate whether it is possible to experimentally control it by varying the amount of light arriving at the dominant and non-dominant eye

title: A normative framework for selective information loss in foveal and peripheral vision
description: [Master's thesis, defended on 04.09.2023 at EPFL, Switzerland] Deep neural networks (DNNs) have reached remarkable proficiency in visual tasks, often surpassing human performance. However, their alignment with human cognitive mechanisms, especially peripheral vision, remains under debate. In humans, peripheral vision, characterized by a decrease in retinal photoreceptor density away from the fovea, is often assumed to be merely more blurry than central vision. Yet, there are reasons to believe that higher cortical processing mechanisms are involved that could explain the selective information loss observed in the periphery of the visual field. This research introduces a novel deep neural network model architecture, composed of autoencoders, as a normative framework to model human peripheral vision. By optimizing the reconstruction of visual input under a constraint on the latent bottleneck, the model aligns with the reduced processing power allocated to peripheral regions in the human visual cortex. Through psychophysical tests, including the honeycomb illusion, pop-out search, and ensemble perception tasks, the model's performance was assessed against human behavior. Results indicated that both humans and the model exhibited similar selective information loss patterns with increasing eccentricity. This work suggests that constrained optimization of a generic image representation objective is a promising approach for understanding human peripheral vision.

title: Predicting Anti–VEGF Treatment Demands and Outcomes for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration (nAMD), Diabetic Macular Oedema (DMO), and Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO)-Associated Macular Oedema U
description: Objective: To map the evidence concerning the use of machine learning (ML) to predict treatment burden and outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema in order to understand the current state of the art and the gaps. Introduction: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD), diabetic macular oedema (DMO), and retinal vein occlusion (RVO) associated macular oedema are some of the leading causes of visual loss globally.1 Intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injections are currently used to treat such diseases.1 The treatment course and outcomes for each patient is variable and thus individualised treatment techniques are needed.2 Two of the most pressing issues are estimating treatment burden (e.g., patients who need fewer vs. more intravitreal injections) and visual prognosis (e.g., good vs. poor responders) in individual patients.2 This research aims to assess the potential of ML to predict treatment burden and outcomes to personalise anti-VEGF treatment in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO. We seek to understand the types of ML approaches that have been explored, their maturity, reported outcomes, and real-world applicability. Eligibility criteria: Studies will be included if they focus on ML algorithms that predict anti-VEGF treatment burden and/or outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema. The included studies will consist of full-length original research journal articles written or translated into English. We will exclude other types of literature (i.e., not full-length journal articles, not a report of original research and not centred on ML algorithms that predict anti-VEGF treatment burden and/or outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema). Publication dates of included studies will be from January 2000 onwards. Methods: Five academic databases will be searched (Ovid Medline, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE, and ACM Digital Library). Search strings for each database were formulated in conjunction with a Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School librarian. Studies will be uploaded to Covidence (literature management software), and duplicates will be removed. Studies will be screened by two independent screeners (SG & AYO). Disagreements will be resolved with a discussion with a third author (DM). SG will conduct a descriptive analysis of the data. We will use the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) for reporting our study, and we will publish our protocol on the Open Science Framework (OSF).3 Results: We will report the number and type of included evidence, as well as any pertinent study characteristics. Main topics of interest and significant outcomes will also be presented. Inferences will be presented in an appropriate diagrammatic or tabular format. Conclusions: Based on the key concepts and topics extrapolated from the selected studies, the scoping review will aim to explore the breadth and depth of the current literature and address any knowledge gaps that can hold the potential to inform future research and future algorithm development. Keywords: Intravitreal injections, ophthalmology, artificial intelligence, systematic scoping review

title: Blood Pressure and the Inner Retina: a Systematic Review of OCT Findings and a Call for Multidisciplinary Glaucoma Management
description: Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy causing retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thinning, retinal ganglion cell (RGC) apoptosis, and visual loss. Accumulating evidence suggests that blood pressure (BP), whether too high or too low, can predispose to negative glaucoma outcomes. Initial hypertensive or hypotensive damage to the RGCs and their axons is a likely explanation. With the constant increase in population and life expectancy, by 2040, the projected number of people with glaucoma worldwide exceeds 110 million, while hypertension already affects approximately one third of the adult population. Nevertheless, the growing disease burden related to the coexistence of glaucoma and suboptimal BP control is currently understated in clinical practice. In this regard, we conducted a systematic review on the relationship between arterial hypertension (AHT) and hypotension with inner retinal thickness, as assessed by structural optical coherence tomography. For this purpose, we searched five databases for studies reporting on BP and the RNFL or ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer thickness (GCIPL) in healthy subjects and in patients with ophthalmic or systemic disease. Findings revealed a U-shaped (or J-shaped) effect, but study design limited the conclusions drawn, especially due to the confounding role of antihypertensive medication. Last, we summarize current AHT treatment standards and call for collaborative management of patients with coexisting glaucomatous and cardiovascular risk.

title: Traditional and novel application of infrared imaging for screening of ocular disorders: a scoping review
description: Near infrared-light based imaging technology is traditionally used for the screening of uncorrected refractive errors (myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism), amblyopia and strabismus. The technology, broadly called photoscreening, involves analysis of the the reflected luminance pattern created across the pupil from light projected onto the retina from an array of infrared LED light source situated below the aperture of an IR sensitive camera. In eyes with regular refractive error, the luminance gradient varies monotonically from brighter to darker from one edge to another edge of the pupil. Apart from these use cases, near infrared imaging techniques have also been reportedly used in the identification of ocular pathologies, such as keratoconus, spasm of near reflex, dry eye, cataract, retinoblastoma, pupillary dysfunction, etc. This technique has also been used in laboratories for measuring the eye's focusing and binocular eye alignment responses. The aim of this scoping review is to understand the traditional application of infrared imaging and the future indications of this technology for screening/detection of ocular disorders.
